author: Kyas Williamson
title: Blockbusters: Who You Gonna Call? Ghostbusters! Opinion | Blockbusters: Who You Gonna Call? Ghostbusters!
text:
Unless you want half of your belongings soaked in ghost plasma while the other half gets destroyed by photon blasts, I wouldn’t recommend calling the Ghostbusters.
In honor of Halloween coming up, I decided this week’s classic should have a spooky twist. Also the name of this film partly inspired my column’s name. Hopefully, in the midst of midterms and Family Weekend, you can find time to relax and enjoy a ghostly film.
It pains me to admit that I saw the 2016 “Ghostbusters” reboot disaster before watching the original. That naive little boy was clueless about the masterpiece that he’d missed out on. Thankfully, I was later enlightened about the error of my ways and introduced to the 1984 “Ghostbusters.”
The movie opens with an unnamed librarian roaming a filing center when a ghost appears and wreaks havoc. In fear, the librarian calls the not-yet-established Ghostbusters, a team which then consists of Dr. Peter Venkman (Bill Murray), Dr. Ray Stantz (Dan Aykroyd) and Dr. Egon Spengler (Harold Ramis).
Inspired by their first ghost sighting, and the loss of their grant funding, the Ghostbusters begin a life of ghoul hunting. Their first official client, Dana Barrett (Sigourney Weaver), asks for their aid after a ghost portal opens in her fridge.
Each ghostbuster has group-defining characteristics. Venkman is flirtatious and witty. Stantz is enthusiastic and open-hearted. Spengler is socially awkward and hyper-intelligent. Winston Zeddemore (Ernie Hudson), who joins the group later, is a grounded, realist everyman.
The film’s main issues stem from these same character traits. Venkman flirts a little too much. While flirting isn’t inherently bad, his interest in Dana becomes a bit creepy. This first happens when Venkman is over at Dana’s apartment investigating paranormal activity. Instead of listening to her concerns, he hits on her the whole time.
There’s a moment where Dana is possessed by a ghost who attempts to sleep with Venkman. While Venkman knows Dana is not herself, he still kisses her a few times. Although he does this to subdue the possessed Dana, it’s still off-putting, to say the least.
Dana and Venkman do have moments of authentic connection. Venkman meets Dana outside her orchestra rehearsal and asks her out. Dana hesitantly accepts. When Venkman rescues Dana towards the end of the film, she elects to kiss him. Their relationship is cute overall, minus Venkman’s weird moments.
Winston is the film’s greatest failure — not his character, but the way the writers display him and his traits. Winston’s character is constantly alienated from the group. He’s not a scientist, and he joined the team last. He’s not even referred to by his last name like the rest of the gang.
Yes, Winston’s supposed to be the everyman whose street smarts contrasts with the group’s book intelligence. Yes, I understand the importance of diverse personalities balancing the group dynamic. However, the film underutilizes these notions, instead presenting Winston purely as an outsider.
Winston also faces physical alienation. Towards the final big battle of the film, the core group looks up at a tall building to see a portal forming at the top, and while Venkman, Stantz and Stegler are standing side by side, Winston is shown behind them. Later on, when the four are blasted away from the villain, Venkman, Stantz and Stegler land together, while Winston ends up alone.
How predictable to alienate the one Black character from the movie’s main group. Winston is often poorly received. In the second season of “Stranger Things,” Lucas Sinclair gets upset with his friends after they force him to be Winston in their group costume. Justice for Winston.
The movie has some great highlights, too. Despite being made in 1984, the CGI holds up. The ghosts don’t look half bad — as long as they don’t move too fast. The proton streams shot from the proton guns have a captivating mix of purple and orange light. Even the giant marshmallow monsters look fluffy, edible and appropriately menacing.
The pacing is fantastic. I only felt the movie drag once, during a montage of the Ghostbusters busting ghosts. The villain is built up slowly throughout the whole film to generate the perfect amount of suspense. The final battle is amazing, although I wish there was a bit more plot afterwards.
The overall plot and story are well-written. The antagonistic and side characters amplify the Ghostbusters and Dana very well. Also, the big bad having ancient origins was a nice touch.
This film is a classic for a reason. Even though it has minor flaws, it’s an enjoyable watch. That theme song is going to be stuck in my head for weeks now.
Kyas Williamson is a Weinberg freshman and author of Blockbusters. He can be contacted at kyaswilliamson2030@u.northwestern.edu .
